title: Three products where four seemed needed
hook: Can two numbers be multiplied with fewer digit products than n × n?

doesNotKnow: that two-digit halves can be multiplied with 3 products instead of 4

misconception: Multiplying two n-digit numbers needs n x n single-digit multiplications and nothing can beat it.
objective: The learner can explain that (a+b)(c+d) - ac - bd gives the cross terms, so each split needs 3 half-size products instead of 4, which compounds to 27 one-digit products against 64 for 11141313 x 13111224 and about n^1.58 against n^2 in general.

claims.text: Multiplying 11141313 by 13111224 down to 1-digit pieces takes 64 one-digit products the schoolbook way and 27 with Karatsuba.
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14, algo2-sc) and school()/kara() in Demo.tsx: real BigInt recursion, split at half the longer length, base case when either factor < 10; counted base-case calls: schoolbook 64, Karatsuba 27; both results equal BigInt 11111111 x 11111111. No half-sum carries (1111 + 1111 = 2222, 11 + 11 = 22, 2 + 2 = 4), so all 27 leaves are truly 1-digit. The same code needs 33 for 12345678 x 87654321 (8765 + 4321 carries), which is why the brief switched numbers (W-179). Stage counts are the trees' real leaves, not constants. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): own node re-implementation of school()/kara() (scratchpad fc22/kara.mjs): leaves 64 and 27, both products equal BigInt 11111111^2; 12345678 x 87654321 gives 33 with Karatsuba, as stated. Stage reveal prints COUNTS[DEPTH]. · v4 (2026-10-14, learner r7: all halves were 1111): example changed to 11141313 x 13111224, picked by builder search (scratchpad g3a0cd_kar.py: random digits 1-4, kept pairs whose Karatsuba leaves are all 1-digit, 27 leaves, 64 schoolbook leaves, and four distinct halves). Builder's Python recursion gives 64 and 27; the example is chosen, disclosed here. Needs re-check. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own node BigInt port of split/school/kara (scratchpad fc26-b0/kara.mjs) on 11141313 x 13111224: schoolbook 64 leaves, Karatsuba 27, all leaves 1-digit, both trees recombine to X*Y. Example choice checked against its stated criteria: every digit is 1-4, the top-split halves 1114, 1313, 1311, 1224 are four distinct values, no Karatsuba leaf exceeds 1 digit. The builder search script itself (g3a0cd_kar.py) was not re-run; the example is disclosed as chosen. Stem and reveal print COUNTS[DEPTH]; no Reset; reduced motion jumps Split down to 1 digit to depth 3, same counts.

claims.text: (a+b)(c+d) = a·c + a·d + b·c + b·d, so one product of the sums minus the two products Karatsuba already has gives both cross terms. For the halves a 1114, b 1313, c 1311, d 1224: a·d + b·c = 1,363,536 + 1,721,343 = 3,084,879, and (a+b)(c+d) - a·c - b·d = 6,152,445 - 1,460,454 - 1,607,112 = 3,084,879.
claims.source: Algebra: (a+b)(c+d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. With a = b = c = d = 1111: 2 x 1,234,321 = 2,468,642 and 2222^2 - 2 x 1,234,321 = 4,937,284 - 2,468,642 = 2,468,642. Computed live on the stage (CROSS and VIA). | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): node: 1111*1111 + 1111*1111 = 2,468,642; 2222^2 - 2*1,234,321 = 4,937,284 - 2,468,642 = 2,468,642. Stage 'Check the middle' line prints CROSS and VIA from the top split. | Builder revision v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): the stage's check line now prints both sides with their parts (stage text 'Schoolbook's a·d + b·c: 1111·1111 + 1111·1111 = 2,468,642' and 'Karatsuba's (a+b)(c+d) − a·c − b·d: 4,937,284 − 1,234,321 − 1,234,321 = 2,468,642', computed in Demo.tsx from the top split), and the reveal quotes the second line. Arithmetic: 2222² = 4,937,284; 1111² = 1,234,321. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own BigInt: split(11111111) at h = 4 gives a = b = c = d = 1111; a·d + b·c = 2,468,642; (a+b)(c+d) = 4,937,284; a·c = b·d = 1,234,321; 4,937,284 - 1,234,321 - 1,234,321 = 2,468,642. Identity holds algebraically ((a+b)(c+d) = ac + ad + bc + bd) and on 10,000 random BigInt quadruples. v3 check lines print TOP.a·TOP.d + TOP.b·TOP.c = fmt(CROSS) and fmt(SUMS) − fmt(AC) − fmt(BD) = fmt(VIA); reveal quotes the second line; milestone middle-checked guarantees it is on stage (no Reset, button disables after). · v4: halves now differ; builder Python: 1114*1224 = 1363536, 1313*1311 = 1721343, sum 3084879; 2427*2535 = 6152445, 1114*1311 = 1460454, 1313*1224 = 1607112, 6152445 - 1460454 - 1607112 = 3084879. Stage computes AD, BC, CROSS, SUMS, AC, BD, VIA live. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own BigInt from split(X, Y), h = 4: a 1114, b 1313, c 1311, d 1224; a*d 1,363,536, b*c 1,721,343, sum 3,084,879; (a+b)(c+d) = 2427*2535 = 6,152,445, a*c 1,460,454, b*d 1,607,112, difference 3,084,879. claims.text: For 1,024-digit numbers, if no half-sum like a+b gains a digit, the count is 59,049 products against 1,048,576 (3^10 against 4^10).
claims.source: 1,024 = 2^10 digits, 10 levels of halving: 3^10 = 59,049 and 4^10 = 1,048,576 (node). Size model: assumes no half-sum carries, as for the stage's numbers; with carries real counts are somewhat higher. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. 3^10 = 59,049 and 4^10 = 1,048,576 are right as an idealised count, but the reveal says 'for 1,024-digit numbers it is 59,049 products', with no 'size model' or 'about'. The lesson's own kara() run on real 1,024-digit inputs (scratchpad fc22/kara.mjs) needs 85,589 / 86,129 / 86,475 one-digit products (three random pairs) and 94,243 for the 1,024-digit repunit, because half-sums carry; schoolbook gives exactly 1,048,576. Fix (builder): say 'in the ideal count with no carries, 3^10 = 59,049 against 4^10 = 1,048,576', or give the real figure ('about 86,000 against 1,048,576'). | Builder fix (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): W-207: reveal now says 'the ideal no-carry count is 59,049 products against 1,048,576 (3^10 against 4^10)', so the figure is labelled as the idealised count; real carried runs are higher (FC measured about 86,000). · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Reveal now says 'the ideal no-carry count is 59,049 products against 1,048,576 (3^10 against 4^10)': 1,024 = 2^10, T(n) = 3T(n/2) with T(1) = 1 gives 3^10 = 59,049, schoolbook 4^10 = 1,048,576. The pass-22 objection (real inputs carry) is met by 'ideal no-carry'. · v4: reveal wording changed from 'the ideal no-carry count' (learner r7: phrase unexplained) to 'if no half-sum like a+b gains a digit'. Same idealised count. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): 1,024 = 2^10; with no half-sum carry every split gives 3 half-size products, T(n) = 3T(n/2), T(1) = 1, so 3^10 = 59,049; schoolbook 4^10 = 1,048,576 (node). Reveal wording 'if no half-sum like a+b gains a digit' states the same no-carry condition that pass 23 accepted.

claims.text: Karatsuba's cost grows about as n^1.58 for n digits, against n^2 for schoolbook.
claims.source: Karatsuba and Ofman 1962 (Doklady Akad. Nauk SSSR); T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) gives Theta(n^log2 3), log2 3 = 1.585. CLRS 4e ch. 4 (problems; chapter only). Citations from memory, not opened. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) gives Theta(n^log2 3), log2 3 = 1.58496 (node); re-derived, so the learner sentence does not rest on an unopened source. Karatsuba & Ofman, Doklady Akad. Nauk SSSR 145(2):293-294 (1962) confirmed bibliographically via search (mathnet.ru record); paper and CLRS not opened.

claims.text: Schoolbook splits each product into 4 half-size products (a·c, a·d, b·c, b·d); Karatsuba uses 3 (a·c, b·d, (a+b)(c+d)).
claims.source: x = a·10^h + b, y = c·10^h + d, so xy = ac·10^2h + (ad + bc)·10^h + bd; Karatsuba gets ad + bc from (a+b)(c+d) - ac - bd. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): algebra re-derived: xy = ac*10^2h + (ad+bc)*10^h + bd; (a+b)(c+d) - ac - bd = ad + bc. Matches the kids lists in school() and kara() and the box labels.

recall.question: Karatsuba multiplies the halves with 3 products instead of 4. Where does the saving come from?
options: (a+b)(c+d) minus a·c and b·d gives both cross terms
It skips the product of the two low halves
It rounds the numbers before multiplying
recall.why: One product of the sums, minus the two products already made, equals a·d + b·c; saving one of four at every level compounds to about n^1.58.
